title: Understanding Implicit Biases in Time-Series Foundation Models
one_liner: Design choices in time-series models like patch size and loss function create unintended hidden side effects that shape how the model handles uncertainty and patterns.
lead: When you train a time-series model, you tweak many dials: how to split the data, how to encode numbers, what loss function to use. Each dial seems like a simple technical choice. But this paper shows that each one carries hidden consequences that ripple through the model's behavior in unintuitive ways. A model trained with one loss function might confidently flatten uncertain predictions; trained with a different loss it might fluidly hop between patterns. The paper maps out these hidden effects so you can predict what will happen when you change a dial.

paras: You build a time-series forecasting model—you want it to predict what happens next in a sequence of measurements (stock prices, temperature, network traffic). You look at benchmarks, pick a few design ingredients to copy: how to slice the data into chunks (called patches), how to convert numbers into internal representations (embedding), and what error-penalty to use during training (the loss function). The model trains, you test it on standard benchmarks, and it works fine.

But here's the problem: when you deploy it on new data that looks different from the benchmark—more chaotic, noisier, with longer time horizons—the same dials that worked before now backfire. The model that learned to be accurate on familiar data suddenly predicts boring, middle-of-the-road forecasts when it should stay responsive. Or it gets tangled in frequency aliasing: when the data's natural patterns do not line up with your patch size, the model scrambles the signal. No one warned you these dials had hidden side effects.

callout.html: Design choices like patch size, embedding type, and loss function quietly reshape how a time-series model handles uncertainty and patterns, in ways that do not show up on standard benchmarks.

steps.text: Slice the data into fixed-size chunks (a dial you choose).
Convert numbers to internal list-of-numbers representation (either exact or rounded to bins).
Pass patches through layers with learned focus (each layer learns which patches matter).
Compare forecast to real data; L2 penalizes large errors uniformly, category-counting does not.
Model now either collapses to mean or stays flexible, depending on the loss choice.

paras: This paper does not invent a new model. Instead, it systematically measures how each dial—patch size, embedding type, loss function—changes the model's internal behavior and its tendency to make certain kinds of predictions. The paper maps the object: the implicit biases (the unintended side effects baked into each design choice).

hidden.name: how hard the model collapses forecasts to the mean
paras: When a model is uncertain, it has to make a choice: hedge its bets by predicting a bland middle-ground, or spread its prediction across multiple futures. Mean-reversion aggressiveness is how strongly the model pulls predictions toward the average. It is a hidden quantity because the paper does not measure it with a single explicit number the model prints out; instead it infers it by looking at how forecasts scatter around the mean in different scenarios.

The paper estimates this quantity by training models with different loss functions and comparing how flat or spiky their forecasts are. A model trained with L2 loss (which penalizes large prediction errors uniformly) tends to aggressively regress to the mean—it learns that predicting the middle is the safest choice. A model trained with cross-entropy loss (which counts categories, like an LLM) does not have this pressure, so it stays looser and more exploratory.

heat.caption: Darker means the model is more aggressive at collapsing forecasts to the mean.

reads.html: Imagine a weather model that always predicts tomorrow will be room temperature no matter the season. That is aggressive mean reversion. A model that says it might be hot, cold, or just right is less aggressive.
Models trained with L2-based loss tend to collapse future variability into a central forecast, while those trained with cross-entropy maintain flexibility to explore multiple forecast modes.

mechanism.h2: Why design choices create these hidden biases
paras: Start with the loss function. During training, the model adjusts its weights (internal numbers) to minimize the error between its forecast and the ground truth. An L2 loss (squared error) punishes large mistakes severely—it says a 10-degree error is 100 times worse than a 1-degree error. This teaches the model to be conservative: predict the middle of the range and avoid extremes, because extreme guesses risk huge penalties. A category-counting loss (used in language models) works differently. It says I predicted category rain, the truth was sunny—one mistake. This loss counts all mistakes equally, so no guess is punished more than any other for being far from the mean. With equal penalties everywhere, the model learns to spread its predictions across multiple futures instead: hot, cold, or medium all cost the same if wrong, so it explores more of the space.

Now add patch size. A patch is a fixed chunk of data you feed to the model at once. If your data has a slow wave (repeats every 100 days) and you use a patch size of 1, the model sees the wave unfold gradually, step by step, and can learn it. But if you use a patch size of 16, and the wave does not align with the boundary every 16 steps, you introduce aliasing: the wave signal scrambles itself at the boundaries. The model sees broken patterns, so the learned focus weights (which pieces of the past matter for forecasting) become bimodal—the model focuses heavily on recent neighbors but barely on distant past, a form of defensive learning.

Finally, embedding type. An exact (continuous) embedding preserves distances: if two numbers are close in value, their internal representations stay close. A rounded (quantized) embedding first sorts numbers into bins, then tries to recover fine detail—it is like photocopying a photo and the photocopy has less detail. This difference means rounded embeddings introduce a bottleneck: the model cannot learn fine-grained patterns as easily, so it defaults to coarser behaviors like mean reversion.

stages.s: Slice into patches (choice: size 1 or 16 or other)
Process through deep layers with learned focusing
Compute loss (choice: L2, L1, or cross-entropy)

math.words: Total loss equals the difference between the forecast and the real value, squared, multiplied by how much the model regresses. Formally: loss = alpha times the sum of the squared forecast errors, where alpha is set by the loss function you choose.
symbols: the model's prediction at time step i
the true value at time step i
add up the squared error for all time steps
total squared error; minimizing it teaches the model to avoid extremes

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose at time step 1: actual = 50, forecast = 60. Error: 60 - 50 = 10. Squared: 10^2 = 100.
At time step 2: actual = 55, forecast = 52. Error: 52 - 55 = -3. Squared: (-3)^2 = 9.
At time step 3: actual = 65, forecast = 53. Error: 53 - 65 = -12. Squared: (-12)^2 = 144.

Total L2 loss = 100 + 9 + 144 = 253. The large error at step 3 dominates. During training, the model learns that extreme forecasts (far from the middle) cause huge penalties, so it shifts strategy toward the middle of the data range.
In contrast, cross-entropy loss would count 1 wrong, 1 wrong, 1 wrong = 3 mistakes, regardless of magnitude. This loss teaches the model to explore multiple futures.

math.note: The squared term in L2 loss punishes distance from the true value; minimizing it teaches the model to predict safe middle values and avoid spreads.

items.html: A model that works perfectly on standard test sets may fail on real data with different frequencies or longer horizons. The design choices that worked for the benchmark data are not forward-compatible.

If the data's recurring patterns do not align with patch boundaries, the model sees scrambled signals and cannot learn the true frequencies. Attention becomes defensive (high on neighbors, low on distant past).

Using L2 or L1 loss on data with multiple valid futures (chaotic dynamics) forces the model to hedge with flat mean-reversion forecasts. Using cross-entropy on a regression task overly rewards exploration and may miss fine-grained tuning.
Quantized embeddings compress information into discrete bins. The model can only partially recover continuous structure, so it defaults to coarse behaviors.
Match your design choices to your data: use cross-entropy loss or quantile loss for chaotic data, choose patch size based on known frequencies, use continuous embeddings if precision matters.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple time-series forecasting task: a dataset with a slow component (a trend) and a fast component (daily oscillation), plus noise. Train two identical models except for the loss function: one with L2 loss, one with cross-entropy loss. On a test split of well-aligned data, both models should perform similarly. On a held-out test set with a longer or noisier horizon, the L2-trained model should show flattened forecasts (aggressive mean reversion), while the cross-entropy model should still spread its predictions. Vary the patch size for a third model: misalign patches so the fast oscillation gets scrambled. Watch the attention weights become bimodal and the forecast accuracy drop.
demo.metric_eq: forecast_spread = variance of predictions over multiple time steps. Mean_reversion_ratio = (forecast_variance - true_data_variance) / true_data_variance. Lower spread and higher ratio = more aggressive mean reversion.
demo.closing: The demo proves that the same small dial (loss function or patch size) invisibly steers the model's forecast strategy, and that the effect is invisible in standard benchmarks but devastating on new data.
